slides: Okay, a quick summary of the fast-calculation toolkit.
Every trick finds an easier calculation, with exactly the same answer.
So, a sum stays the same when you move an amount from one part to the other.
And a difference stays the same when you add the same amount to both numbers.
Don't mix them up. That's the trap.
Split one factor into easy pieces.
Times eleven: that's times ten, plus one copy. Times nine: times ten, minus one copy.
Halve one factor, double the other. The product doesn't move.
So fourteen halves to seven. Forty-five doubles to ninety. Seven nineties... six thirty.
Now, divide first, and the numbers stay small.
Round to a hundred, then correct.
A hundred thirty-sixes is thirty-six hundred. That's two thirty-sixes too many... so, seventy-two.
Rounded up? The easy product is too big, so subtract. Rounded down? Add.
Look for pairs that make a round number: four and twenty-five, eight and one twenty-five, two and fifty, five and twenty.
Now, cancel only when the top and the bottom are products. A plus on top? No cancelling.
Evenly around a centre: the centre squared, minus the gap squared. But the gaps must be equal.
Front digit times the next number, then twenty-five on the end. And this is only for squares.
You may swap the two numbers. So pick the easier one.
Use exactly as much precision as the choices need. Only one choice left? Stop.
Okay, before you practice, ask yourself these questions.
The traps: shifting a sum the wrong way, cancelling across a plus, and using the centre trick with unequal gaps.
And if nothing looks easier... well, a clean written calculation is a great answer too.
